target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would broadly reduce work/school barriers and thus increase turnout
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically give private-sector workers the day off or paid leave, so the people most constrained by work—especially low-income hourly workers in retail and service jobs—may still have to work and may even face added costs. Therefore, the holiday is not a reliable way to remove the main voting barrier for those voters.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday must legally force private employers to close in order to reduce barriers
objection: A national Election Day holiday can still reduce scheduling barriers even without mandating paid leave, because many schools and workplaces shift to holiday schedules, freeing substantial time for employees and students to vote.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would meaningfully increase turnout on its own
objection: Research suggests that an Election Day holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with other voting-access reforms, so a calendar change alone is unlikely to produce a meaningful turnout increase.

target: AG2's claim that broad domestic support and OECD practice are irrelevant to effectiveness
objection: Bipartisan support and the fact that many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays are evidence that the reform is workable and can plausibly increase turnout, not just a symbolic gesture.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday would not meaningfully increase turnout on its own because some barriers remain
objection: Reducing the work/school scheduling barrier alone is enough to make voting more feasible for many eligible voters, so a holiday can meaningfully increase turnout even without other reforms.

target: AG1's assumption that removing scheduling barriers is enough despite unchanged election operations
objection: A holiday changes the calendar but does not automatically increase polling-place staffing or fix operational bottlenecks, so longer lines and wait times can offset any scheduling gains and limit turnout effects.

target: AG2's claim that unchanged polling operations undermine the holiday's value
objection: The holiday still meaningfully improves access for voters whose main barrier is work or school attendance, so the absence of automatic operational fixes does not negate its barrier-reduction effect.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday addresses the relevant barriers to voting
objection: Many voters also face administrative and eligibility barriers, such as registration or being recognized in the system, and a holiday does not fix those obstacles; reforms like automatic voter registration directly do so and are therefore more reliable.

target: AG2's claim that unresolved administrative barriers undermine the holiday proposal
objection: A policy can still be justified by removing the major scheduling barrier it targets, even if it does not solve every administrative or eligibility problem at once.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday reliably removes the main voting constraint
objection: A calendar holiday does not reliably remove the concrete constraints that keep eligible people from voting, because it does not guarantee usable time, fix election operations, or remove administrative hurdles.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday is unreliable because it does not solve every barrier
objection: For many eligible voters, the key constraint is having to attend work or school on Election Day, and a national holiday does reliably remove that specific scheduling constraint for them.

target: AG1's claim that school closures and holiday schedules will substantially reduce barriers in practice
objection: Although schools may close, the reform still depends on workplace and private-employer decisions, and the holiday does not legally require private employers to provide paid time off or close, so many workers—especially hourly workers—may still have to work.

target: AG2's claim that popularity and OECD practice do not support the reform
objection: Broad support in the U.S. and common practice in comparable democracies are evidence that the holiday is administratively workable and typically changes school/work schedules enough to matter for access.

target: AG1's claim that holiday schedules will help low-income workers
objection: Private employers, especially in retail and service sectors, are not required to close or give paid time off, so many low-income hourly workers would still be scheduled to work and would not reliably gain time to vote; the holiday could even worsen inequities for them.

target: AG2's claim that low-income workers won't benefit from holiday scheduling changes
objection: Holiday designation often reduces staffing or shifts hours in ways that can create usable time windows even for hourly workers, so it can ease work/school attendance burdens for many low-income workers.

target: AG1's claim that civic framing itself boosts turnout
objection: Voting turnout depends on practical ability to vote, not just whether civic participation feels more important; a holiday mostly changes calendar and symbolism without ensuring people can actually cast ballots.

target: AG2's claim that symbolic framing is ineffective
objection: When a holiday creates usable time to vote and makes participation feel more important, voters are more likely to take up that opportunity, so the celebration framing can increase turnout rather than just being symbolic.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday would help the people most constrained by schedules
objection: For many low-income hourly workers in private-sector jobs, a federal holiday does not require employers to close or pay them to stay home, so it does not reliably create usable voting time and may impose extra costs instead.

target: AG2's claim that low-income workers would not benefit and that civic framing is too weak
objection: Holiday schedules can still reduce the work burden for some hourly workers, and if the holiday eases scheduling barriers even partially, framing voting as a civic celebration can help more of them act on the opportunity to vote.

target: AG1's claim that broad support and holiday framing make the reform worthwhile
objection: Research indicates that making Election Day a holiday by itself is unlikely to increase turnout meaningfully, and the expected benefit is small or unreliable compared with the burdens that fall disproportionately on low-income workers.

target: AG2's claim that holiday status won't meaningfully change work schedules
objection: Even without a paid-leave mandate, holiday designation typically changes school and workplace schedules enough to create usable time windows for many voters, including hourly workers.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday will help low-income workers and improve turnout
objection: Because a federal holiday does not require most private employers to close or provide paid leave, many low-income hourly workers would still be required to work, so the holiday would not reliably remove their main barrier to voting.

target: AG1's broader claim that the holiday is the best access strategy
objection: In sectors like retail and service, holiday demand can keep or even increase work obligations, meaning a holiday may maintain or worsen the scheduling constraints that block voting for low-income workers; more direct reforms like employer time-off laws or automatic voter registration are better.

target: AG2's claim that school-based constraints are irrelevant to the holiday proposal
objection: School attendance is also a major voting barrier, and a national holiday would reduce school attendance obligations, creating usable time for voters tied to school schedules, such as parents and guardians.

target: AG1's claim that school closures make the holiday broadly effective
objection: Even if schools close, many of the most constrained voters are low-income hourly workers whose private employers still may schedule them to work; easing school-related constraints does not reliably translate into usable voting time for those workers.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday is too weak to matter because it does not fix every barrier
objection: The holiday reduces routine attendance obligations through school closures and altered workplace schedules, which creates usable time to vote for many people and can improve participation even if it does not solve every non-scheduling barrier.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday-by-itself mechanism is sufficient
objection: Research says that an Election Day holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with reforms that directly remove voting barriers, so relying mainly on a holiday is unlikely to produce a meaningful turnout increase.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday is merely symbolic
objection: A national holiday directly changes work and school attendance conditions, so it is not purely symbolic; it reduces major scheduling barriers and can plausibly produce meaningful turnout gains when combined with civic-importance framing.
